body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how muckraking journalism moved Congress to regulate food and drugs, and evaluate the role of the press in reform (D2.His.14.9-12, RH.9-10.1).
- Students explain how the Sixteenth, Seventeenth and Nineteenth Amendments changed the powers of government and the role of citizens (D2.Civ.4.9-12, D2.Civ.14.9-12).
- Students argue which Progressive reform had the greatest long-term impact, weighing it against an alternative (D2.His.14.9-12, D4.1.9-12, WHST.9-10.1).
- Students identify the limits of Progressive reform, especially for Black Americans in the segregated South (D2.His.4.9-12).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: The Jungle and Sinclair's reflection, Roosevelt's "Man with the Muck-rake," the Progressive Amendments, the Progressive Era Reforms reference card
- The class discussion "Should the government regulate big business?" (from the showcase class, if your district has it)
- Chart paper for a reform gallery walk: Problem, Reformers, Tool, Result, Who was left out
- Optional: public-domain photographs of child laborers by Lewis Hine (Library of Congress)

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Reformers and Their Targets. Connect to Unit 3: which problems from the Gilded Age readings are still unsolved in 1900? Begin the lesson activity, Muckrakers and Lawmakers, with the Sinclair reading.
Day 2: Finish Muckrakers and Lawmakers with the Roosevelt and amendment readings. Debrief: why did Sinclair's book change food law but not working conditions? Introduce the essay The Most Important Progressive Reform and the reference card.
Day 3: Reform gallery walk: groups make a chart for one reform (consumer protection, antitrust, amendments, labor, conservation, civil rights organizing). Students choose their essay reform and the alternative they will argue against. Optional class discussion on regulating business.
Day 4: Essay workshop: thesis conferences and a mini-lesson on "weighing alternatives" (concede, then show why your reform still matters more). Students draft.
Day 5: Unit assessment: Progressive Era Document Check (no AI help). Essays are due at the end of the following week.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a reform-choice organizer: the reform, the problem it solved, two pieces of evidence, the long-term effect today, and the alternative.
- Support: read the amendment texts aloud and paraphrase each together in one plain sentence before students answer questions about them.
- Extension: research Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) and how child labor was finally regulated in the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), connecting to Unit 6.
- Extension: read a short public-domain piece by Ida B. Wells (Southern Horrors, 1892) and argue whether she belongs at the center of the Progressive story.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): pre-teach the legal words with a three-column chart (word, plain meaning, example): amendment, regulate, monopoly, suffrage, abridge. Allow essays to begin with a bilingual outline.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are now studying the Progressive Era, about 1890 to 1920, when reformers fought for safe food, fair elections, limits on monopolies and women's right to vote. Many laws we still live with, such as federal food inspection and the income tax, date from these years. Ask your student which Progressive reform they think mattered most, and whether you agree. Thank you for talking history at home.
title: Teacher guide: The Progressive Era
